                                                           Abstract
      We consider the problem of minimizing different notions of swap regret in online optimization.
      These forms of regret are tightly connected to correlated equilibrium concepts in games, and have
      been more recently shown to guarantee non-manipulability against strategic adversaries. The only
      computationally efficient algorithm for minimizing linear swap regret over a general convex set
      in Rd was developed recently by Daskalakis, Farina, Fishelson, √ Pipis, and Schneider (STOC ’25).
      However, it incurs a highly suboptimal regret bound of Ω(d4 T ) and also relies on computationally
      intensive calls to the ellipsoid algorithm at each iteration.
           In this paper,

      antees O(d T ) linear swap regret for a general convex set that has been preconditioned via the
      John ellipsoid. Our algorithm leverages the powerful response-based approachability framework
      of Bernstein and Shimkin (JMLR ’15)—previously overlooked in the line of work on swap re-
      gret minimization—and simultaneously minimizes profile swap regret, which was recently shown

1. Introduction
Online optimization provides a framework for sequential decision making under uncertainty. In
this setting, a learner repeatedly selects a strategy from a convex set P ⊂ Rd , while an adversary
specifies a loss function. Although standard algorithms, such as online gradient descent (Zinke-
vich, 2003) and multiplicative weights update (Littlestone and Warmuth, 1994), minimize external
regret—comparing the learner’s performance relative to the best fixed strategy in hindsight—this
metric is often inadequate in complex dynamic environments. To address this, various strengthen-
ings of external regret have been put forward. Φ-regret stands out as a central notion for capturing
advanced forms of hindsight rationality (Stoltz and Lugosi, 2007; Greenwald and Jafari, 2003).

     Unlike external regret, which juxtaposes the performance of the learner against a static compara-
tor, Φ-regret compares against a dynamic sequence of strategies produced by applying a transforma-
tion ϕ : P → P from a set Φ to the learner’s history of play. A learner experiences low Φ-regret if
no consistent modification of their past behavior—induced by some transformation ϕ ∈ Φ—would
significantly reduce their cumulative loss. When Φ comprises all affine transformations mapping P
to itself, this is known as linear swap regret. Φ-regret has an intrinsic appeal as a general and robust
performance measure in online learning, and has found many important applications in other areas.
     Indeed, Φ-regret has been a mainstay in algorithmic game theory, where it is deeply connected to
fundamental solution concepts. A celebrated result establishes that if all players employ algorithms
that minimize swap regret, the average correlated distribution of play converges to the set of corre-
lated equilibria (Foster and Vohra, 1997; Hart and Mas-Colell, 2000; Stoltz and Lugosi, 2005; Blum
and Mansour, 2007), a seminal notion introduced by Aumann (1974). More broadly, no-Φ-regret
learning guarantees convergence to the set of Φ-equilibria (Stoltz and Lugosi, 2007; Greenwald and
Jafari, 2003). While the early foundational work focused on the probability simplex, corresponding
to normal-form games, there has been a surge of recent research exploring Φ-regret minimization in
games with more complex strategy sets, most notably extensive-form games (see also Section A).
     Swap regret has also been linked to non-manipulability against a strategic adversary (Deng
et al., 2019). In fact, Arunachaleswaran et al. (2024) showed that, in stark contrast to mean-based
algorithms such as multiplicative weights update, no-swap-regret algorithms are, in some sense,
Pareto optimal. The scope of this line of work has expanded to general polytope games (Mansour
et al., 2022), culminating in the recent introduction of profile swap regret by Arunachaleswaran
et al. (2025). Crucially, while minimizing full swap regret is intractable in the online learning set-
ting (Daskalakis et al., 2024), Arunachaleswaran et al. (2025) established that there are efficient
algorithms for minimizing profile swap regret. Moreover, minimizing this metric suffices to guar-
antee that the learner cannot be manipulated by a strategic adversary.
     From a computational point of view, developing efficient online algorithms to minimize Φ-regret
has been a formidable challenge. The first polynomial-time algorithm for minimizing linear swap
regret over general convex sets was established only recently√ by Daskalakis et al. (2025). How-
ever,  their algorithm  yields a weak  regret bound  of Ω(d 4 T ); this stands in stark contrast to the

    A general framework for minimizing Φ-regret was developed by Gordon et al. (2008). It distills
the basic ingredients of earlier constructions—in the special case where P is a probability simplex—
by Blum and Mansour (2007) and Stoltz and Lugosi (2005). Specifically, the reduction of Gordon

6. Conclusions and future research
We introduced a new unifying approach for minimizing different notions of swap regret by con-
necting to the response-based approachability framework of Bernstein and Shimkin (2015). Com-
pared to previous work of Daskalakis et al. (2025), the resulting algorithm attains an improved
regret
     √ bound and is also computationally more efficient. Moreover, we established a matching
Ω(d T ) lower bound for linear swap regret, establishing for the first time that the classic algorithm
of Gordon et al. (2008) is existentially optimal for that metric, although it is computationally in-
tractable (Daskalakis et al., 2025). An interesting question is to obtain stronger lower bounds for
a set of swap deviations with polynomial dimension, such as low-degree polynomials. Moreover,
our focus has been on the regime where

that one can improve over the Ω(d T ) barrier in the high dimensional regime by leveraging recent

Appendix A. Further related work
The notion of linear swap regret—as a relaxation of full swap regret—was introduced by Gordon
et al. (2008). The first efficient algorithm for minimizing linear swap regret in extensive-form games
was provided more recently by Farina and Pipis (2023). In that setting, linear swap regret subsumes
weaker notions of regret (Farina et al., 2022) linked to extensive-form correlated and coarse cor-
related equilibria (von Stengel and Forges, 2008; Farina et al., 2020). A natural interpretation of
linear correlated equilibria based on a mediator was later provided by Zhang et al. (2024b) (cf. Fujii,
2025). Daskalakis et al. (2025) observed that when the underlying strategy set P is given explicitly
as a polytope, there is an efficient membership oracle that ascertains whether a purported affine
endomorphism is indeed one. By standard reductions (Grötschel et al., 1993), this enables efficient
optimization over End(P), and thereby efficient regret minimization. When P is given explicitly
as a polytope, Zhang et al. (2025a) provided an explicit representation of the set End(P), which
enables efficient algorithms without relying on ellipsoid.
     Algorithms for minimizing Φ-regret have traditionally either followed the template of Gordon
et al. (2008), or rely on the approachability framework of Blackwell (1956). While these approaches
are in a certain sense equivalent (Abernethy et al., 2011), there is nuance to this equivalence (Dann
et al., 2025). A new algorithmic approach for minimizing swap regret was recently introduced
by Peng and Rubinstein (2024) and Dagan et al. (2024), but    √ their reduction is only meaningful in
the very high dimensional regime. Interestingly, our Ω(d T ) lower bound for linear swap regret
only applies √ when T ≥ Ω(d4 ); it is possible that in the high dimensional regime one can improve
over our O(d T ) upper bound using some variation of the approach of Peng and Rubinstein (2024);
Dagan et al. (2024) tailored to linear swap regret.
     Tracing back to the work of Foster and Vohra (1997), it has been known that swap regret is
intimately connected to calibration. This connection was further cultivated in recent work that
addressed the complexity of calibration in high dimensions (Fishelson et al., 2025; Peng, 2025).
Relatedly, the notion of swap regret has found fertile ground in the line of work on multicalibra-
tion (Hébert-Johnson et al., 2018) and omniprediction (Gopalan et al., 2021, 2023).
     The famous theorem of John (1948) states that every compact and convex set with nonempty
interior has a unique maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid—known as the John ellipsoid. This
concept has been a mainstay in convex geometry (Ball, 1991, 2001; Lutwak et al., 2005; Todd,
2016), and has many important algorithmic applications (e.g., Lee and Sidford, 2014; Hazan and
Karnin, 2016; Nikolov et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2024).
